statement: Meroitic script exists in two forms, both derived from Egyptian writing: hieroglyphic (columnar, monumental), descended from Egyptian hieroglyphs, and cursive (horizontal, right-to-left, the majority of surviving texts), descended from Egyptian demotic. Francis Llewellyn Griffith (Oxford) established the phonetic values of the 23-sign script between 1909 and 1911, using bilingual/onomastic evidence (Meroitic royal names cross-matched against Egyptian hieroglyphic renderings, and funerary formulas invoking Isis/Osiris whose Egyptian pronunciation was known). This is a strong PARTIAL-decipherment example: the phonetic values are read reliably, but the Meroitic language remained only partly understood for decades until Claude Rilly (CNRS) demonstrated it belongs to a Nilo-Saharan branch he named Northern East Sudanic, alongside Nubian, Nara, Taman, and Nyima (Rilly and de Voogt, The Meroitic Language and Writing System, Cambridge University Press, 2012), ending a century of dispute about the language's affiliation.
